newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis ends first week, Japan sees long wait.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis ends first week, Japan sees long wait.

text.p: More than 140 hostages faced a bleak Christmas in Lima on Tuesday as captives of Marxist rebels, and Japan's prime minister said the week-old crisis could drag on into 1997.

Following the release on Sunday night of 225 hostages as a "Christmas gesture," the guerrillas were silent. Captives still held at the Japanese ambassador's residence included Peruvian cabinet ministers, senior Japanese diplomats and businessmen, President Alberto Fujimori's brother and a number of Latin American ambassadors.

In Hamburg, Germany, a man claiming to be the international spokesman for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement said the rebels who seized the diplomatic residence on Dec. 17 during a cocktail party would never surrender.

"Effectively, what the government of President (Albert) Fujimori is asking is that the group ... gives up," said Isaac Velzaco in a television interview with Cable News Network. "The word surrender or capitulation is not in the vocabulary of the Tupac Amaru soldier."
Earlier on Monday, a woman claiming to be Velazco's wife, Norma Velazco, called a Paraguayan radio station from Hamburg claiming the MRTA was planning more attacks.
Police sources in Lima told Reuters they believed another clandestine MRTA commando unit was at large in the Peruvian capital and could strike if dialogue breaks down.

Fujimori, in his only words to the public since the siege began, told the rebels he would not use force and would consider a peaceful "way out" if they laid down their arms and gave up all their hostages.
In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto predicted the crisis would be a drawn-out affair and cancelled an important visit by his foreign minister to South Korea.
"I think it will take time (to resolve the crisis)," Hashimoto told reporters on Tuesday shortly after speaking by telephone to Peru's Fujimori.
"The fact that it will take time means that no get-tough approach will be taken," Hashimoto said.
"Taking a long time means that the Peruvian government will not resort to forceful measures," he said. "We are braced for a long haul, even if the New Year holiday is ruined."

Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who scrapped his South Korea trip to concentrate on the hostage crisis, also announced on Tuesday that Japan would hire more security guards to protect its diplomatic offices overseas from terrorist attack.
Popular anger in Japan boiled over into immigrant bashing in Isezaki, an industrial town north of Tokyo, where shops and cars owned by Peruvians were stoned.
The Peruvian community in and around Isezaki, made up largely of Peruvians of Japanese descent, is perhaps the largest in Japan, accounting for about 4,000 of the 15,000 Peruvians in the country.
"I'm really disappointed by the Japanese," Peruvian-Japanese grocery store owner Pedro Nishimata told Reuters. "I thought the Japanese were more mature."

In Peru, the government kept electricity and telephone services to the building cut on Tuesday, although water service was expected to be resumed after released hostages said that lack of water in the residence was endangering the health and safety of those still inside.

Red Cross officials also said they planned to set up a clinic inside the compound later on Tuesday to deal with medical problems among the hostages, which include cases of eye infection and diarrhoea.

The rebels, led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, a textile worker turned revolutionary, have demanded that the government free their jailed MRTA comrades before ending the siege, but Fujimori has flatly refused.

The rebels have booby-trapped the entrances of the building and carry backpacks full of explosives. Police say the guerrillas include four sharpshooters at strategic windows armed with telescopic night-sight rifles.
The Red Cross, which sent in Christmas cakes and other food to feed the captives, said it planned to send them "something special" -- perhaps a Christmas dinner -- on Tuesday evening.
It was not clear if the rebels would permit the gift, however.
